Find an integral expression for the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=1-t, \quad y= \dfrac{2}{3} t^{3/2}, \qquad t\in[0,1].
$$

decisions.question: e-602

source.question: e-602
source.value:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})={t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(-1)}^{2}+{({t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡t))=-\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+{tan}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x=e^t(\cos{t}+\sin{t}), \quad y=e^t(\cos{t}-\sin{t}) , \quad t\in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right].
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14010979/assets/15d185178bf8882f837c19361d630c0e537e145ca2337cad4655677255d0348a.png)

decisions.question: e-603

source.question: e-603
source.value:
Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$
